modules.title: Introduction to the SketchUp Interface
modules.content:
## Imagine Your First 3D Space

Imagine you are standing in the middle of a completely empty, infinite white room. There are no walls, no ceiling, and no floor—just a vast void. However, as you look down, you see three brightly colored lines meeting at a single point beneath your feet: one red, one green, and one blue.

These lines are your only landmarks. In the physical world, we rely on gravity and horizons to tell us which way is "up." In a 3D software environment, you are the god of your own universe, and those colored lines are your compass. If you can master how to move your eyes around this void and understand what those lines are telling you, you have already overcome the steepest part of the learning curve in 3D modeling.

SketchUp is designed to feel like sketching on paper, but with the added dimension of depth. Before you can draw a single line or build a house, you must first learn how to "walk" through this digital space.

## Understanding the 3D Viewport

The majority of your screen is taken up by the **Viewport**. This is the active 3D area where your models live. Unlike a 2D drawing program (like Paint or Photoshop) where you move a flat piece of paper, the Viewport is a window into a three-dimensional world.

Because you are looking at a 3D world on a 2D screen, you need a way to change your perspective. This is called **Navigation**.

### The Three Pillars of Navigation

To move around your model, you will use three primary motions: Orbit, Pan, and Zoom. Mastering these is the difference between fighting with the software and flowing with it.

**1. Orbit (Rotating your view)**
Orbiting allows you to rotate the camera around a central point. Think of it as walking in a circle around a sculpture to see it from the back or the side.
*   **How to do it:** Click the **Orbit tool** (the icon with two green arrows forming a circle) or, more efficiently, click and hold the **Middle Mouse Button (Scroll Wheel)**.
*   **The Feel:** As you move the mouse, the world rotates. This is how you discover the "depth" of your object.

**2. Pan (Sliding your view)**
Panning moves the camera linearly—up, down, left, or right—without rotating it. If Orbiting is like walking around a sculpture, Panning is like sliding your chair across the floor to get a better look at a specific detail.
*   **How to do it:** Click the **Pan tool** (the icon with a hand) or hold **Shift + Middle Mouse Button**.
*   **The Feel:** The entire scene slides in the direction of your mouse.

**3. Zoom (Changing the scale)**
Zooming brings you closer to an object or pushes you further away.
*   **How to do it:** Use the **Scroll Wheel** on your mouse to zoom in and out.
*   **The Pro Tip:** SketchUp zooms toward your cursor. If you want to zoom in on a specific window of a house, place your mouse cursor directly over that window before scrolling.

### Scenario: The "Lost in Space" Moment
It is common for beginners to accidentally Orbit or Pan too far, leaving their screen completely blank. You’ve "flown" away from your model into the void. When this happens, don't panic. 
*   Go to the menu: **Camera > Zoom Extents**. 
*   This command instantly snaps the camera back so that everything you have drawn fits perfectly within the window.

## The Layout: Toolbars and the Large Tool Set

SketchUp provides several ways to access its functions. While there are menus at the top of the screen, professional users rely on **Toolbars** for speed.

### The Large Tool Set
By default, SketchUp may show a small, condensed set of tools. However, for beginners, the **Large Tool Set** is the gold standard. It places all the essential drawing and navigation tools in a vertical bar on the left side of the screen.

**To enable it:** Go to **View > Toolbars** and check the box for **Large Tool Set**.

The Large Tool Set is organized into logical groups:
*   **Top Section:** Navigation tools (Orbit, Pan, Zoom).
*   **Middle Section:** Drawing tools (Lines, Rectangles, Circles).
*   **Bottom Section:** Modification tools (Move, Rotate, Scale).

### The Measurements Box (The VCB)
In the bottom right corner of your screen, you will see a small box. This is the **Value Control Box (VCB)**. 

This is one of the most important parts of the interface. You do not "click" inside this box to type. Instead, you perform an action (like drawing a line), type a number on your keyboard, and hit **Enter**. The VCB tells the software exactly how long or how large you want an object to be.

## Configuring Your Workspace: Templates and Units

Before you start building, you must tell SketchUp what "language" of measurement you are speaking. A 10-unit wall means something very different if the unit is *millimeters* versus *meters*.

### Choosing a Template
When you first open SketchUp, you are prompted to choose a **Template**. A template is a pre-configured set of settings that determines the background color, the default style, and the units of measurement.

*   **Architectural Templates:** Usually set to Feet and Inches or Meters. These are best for buildings and interior design.
*   **Simple Templates:** Often set to Millimeters or Centimeters. These are better for product design or small-scale jewelry.

**How to change your template:**
If you started in the wrong units, you don't need to restart. Go to **Window > Model Info > Units**. Here, you can toggle between:
*   **Architectural:** (e.g., 10' 6")
*   **Decimal:** (e.g., 10.5')
*   **Precision:** You can decide how many decimal places you want (e.g., 0.00m vs 0.0000m).

## Managing the Axes: Navigating 3D Space

In a 2D program, you have an X-axis (horizontal) and a Y-axis (vertical). In 3D, we add the Z-axis (depth). SketchUp uses a color-coded system to make this intuitive.

### The Color Code
The lines you see crossing at the center of your screen are the **Axes**. They are the "North, South, East, and West" of your digital world.

*   **The Red Axis:** Represents one horizontal direction (usually thought of as Left/Right).
*   **The Green Axis:** Represents the other horizontal direction (usually thought of as Forward/Backward).
*   **The Blue Axis:** Represents the vertical direction (Up/Down).

### Why Axes Matter
The axes are not just visual guides; they are "magnetic" anchors. When you eventually start drawing, SketchUp will use these colors to tell you if your line is perfectly straight. 

If you are drawing a line and it turns **Red**, the software is telling you: *"This line is perfectly parallel to the Red Axis."* If the line is black, it is skewed or diagonal. Understanding this color-coding prevents your models from looking "crooked" or slanted.

### Changing the Axis Orientation
Sometimes, you may find that the "ground" is facing the wrong way for your specific project. You can right-click on any of the axes in the viewport to flip them or change their orientation, though for beginners, it is recommended to leave them in the default position until you are comfortable with 3D navigation.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Navigation is a Trio:** Use **Orbit** (rotate), **Pan** (slide), and **Zoom** (scale) to move through your 3D space.
*   **Mouse Shortcuts:** The Middle Mouse Button is your most powerful tool for navigation (Hold for Orbit, Shift+Hold for Pan).
*   **Large Tool Set:** Enable this via **View > Toolbars** to keep all essential tools visible on the left.
*   **The VCB:** The Measurements box in the bottom right is used for precision; type your values and hit Enter.
*   **Template Setup:** Set your units (Meters, Inches, etc.) in **Window > Model Info > Units** before starting a project.
*   **The Color Compass:** 
    *   **Red** = Horizontal X
    *   **Green** = Horizontal Y
    *   **Blue** = Vertical Z

modules.title: Drawing 2D Shapes and Lines
modules.content:
## The Secret to 3D is a Perfect 2D Plan

Imagine you are building a house. You wouldn't start by haphazardly stacking bricks in the air; you would start with a blueprint—a flat, precise 2D drawing of the floor plan. 

SketchUp works exactly the same way. While the software is famous for its 3D capabilities, every 3D object begins as a 2D shape. A skyscraper is just a rectangle that was pulled upward; a coffee mug is just a circle that was stretched. If your 2D foundation is crooked or imprecise, your 3D model will be unstable and frustrating to work with.

To master SketchUp, you must first master the art of the "flat" drawing.

## Precision with the Line Tool

The **Line tool** (shortcut: **L**) is the most fundamental tool in your arsenal. It allows you to create **Edges**—the lines that define the boundaries of your objects. 

### Understanding the Axis System
Before you click, look at the three colored lines intersecting in the center of your viewport. These are the **Axes**, and they are your primary guide for precision:
*   **Red Axis:** Represents the East-West direction (Width).
*   **Green Axis:** Represents the North-South direction (Depth).
*   **Blue Axis:** Represents Up and Down (Height).

When you draw a line, SketchUp tries to "snap" your cursor to these axes. When the line you are drawing turns red, green, or blue, it means you are drawing perfectly parallel to that axis. This is called **Inference**.

### Axis Locking
Sometimes, the software might guess the wrong direction, or you might be drawing at an angle and want to force the line to go perfectly straight. This is where **Axis Locking** comes in. While the Line tool is active, use the arrow keys on your keyboard to lock your direction:
*   **Right Arrow:** Locks the line to the **Red Axis**.
*   **Left Arrow:** Locks the line to the **Green Axis**.
*   **Up Arrow:** Locks the line to the **Blue Axis**.

Once a line is locked, it will stay in that direction regardless of how you move your mouse, until you click to set the endpoint.

### Drawing Your First Line
1. Select the **Line tool** from the Large Tool Set.
2. Click once in the viewport to set the starting point.
3. Move your mouse in the direction you want the line to go.
4. Click a second time to set the endpoint.

## Entering Exact Dimensions

Clicking and dragging is great for sketching, but professional modeling requires mathematical precision. You should almost never "eye-ball" the length of a line.

### Using the Measurements Box
In the bottom right corner of your screen, you will see the **Measurements box** (which functions as the Value Control Box for these tools). 

**Crucial Rule:** You do not click inside the Measurements box. You simply type while the tool is active.

**The Workflow for Precise Lines:**
1. Start the **Line tool**.
2. Click once to start the line.
3. Move your mouse in the desired direction (use Axis Locking to ensure it's straight).
4. Type the exact length (e.g., `5'6"` or `1.5m` depending on your Template).
5. Press **Enter**.

SketchUp will instantly snap the line to that exact length. If you realize the line is too short after you've clicked, you can still type a new dimension and press Enter immediately after, and the line will update.

## Creating Basic Shapes

While you can draw a rectangle using four individual lines, SketchUp provides dedicated tools to create common shapes faster.

### The Rectangle Tool (Shortcut: R)
The **Rectangle tool** creates four connected lines and a **Face**. A **Face** is the flat surface that fills the area between closed lines. Without a face, you have a wireframe; with a face, you have a surface that can eventually be turned into a 3D volume.

1. Select the **Rectangle tool**.
2. Click once to set the first corner.
3. Move your mouse to define the size.
4. To be precise, type the width and height separated by a comma (e.g., `10', 12'`) and press **Enter**.

### The Circle Tool (Shortcut: C)
Circles in SketchUp are actually made of many short, straight line segments (called **Segments**). The more segments a circle has, the smoother it looks.

1. Select the **Circle tool**.
2. Click to set the center point of the circle.
3. Move your mouse outward to define the **Radius** (the distance from the center to the edge).
4. Type the radius (e.g., `3'`) and press **Enter**.

*Pro Tip: If you want a smoother circle, look at the Measurements box immediately after selecting the tool. It will say "Sides." Type a higher number (like `48` or `60`) and press Enter before you start drawing.*

### The Polygon Tool
The **Polygon tool** is used for shapes with equal sides, such as hexagons or octagons.

1. Select the **Polygon tool**.
2. Click to set the center point.
3. Move your mouse to define the radius.
4. Type the radius and press **Enter**.
5. Just like the circle, you can change the number of sides by typing a number (e.g., `6` for a hexagon) and pressing Enter before you click to start the shape.

## Using the Tape Measure for Construction Guides

In the real world, carpenters use pencils to draw "layout lines" on wood before they cut. In SketchUp, we use the **Tape Measure tool** (shortcut: **T**) to create **Guides**.

**Guides** are dashed lines that do not form part of your actual geometry. They are invisible to the final "physical" object but essential for planning.

### Creating Guide Lines
1. Select the **Tape Measure tool**.
2. Hover over an existing edge or axis.
3. Click once and drag the cursor away from the edge.
4. You will see a dashed line appear. 
5. Type the exact distance you want the guide to be from the edge (e.g., `2'`) and press **Enter**.

### Why use Guides?
Guides are invaluable for:
*   **Consistent Spacing:** If you are drawing a row of windows, use guides to mark exactly where each one starts.
*   **Centering:** Create guides to find the exact midpoint of a wall before drawing a door.
*   **Alignment:** Ensure that multiple shapes are perfectly lined up across your drawing.

*Note: Because guides are only for planning, you can delete them later by selecting them with the Select tool and pressing Delete, or by going to Edit > Delete Guides.*

## Realistic Scenario: Mapping a Room Floor

Let's put these tools together to create a precise 2D floor plan for a small 10' x 12' room with a 3' wide doorway.

1. **The Perimeter:** Select the **Rectangle tool**. Click once, type `10', 12'`, and press **Enter**. You now have a closed loop with a face.
2. **Locating the Door:** We need the door to start exactly 2 feet from the left wall. Select the **Tape Measure tool**. Click on the left edge of the rectangle, drag to the right, type `2'`, and press **Enter**. You now have a dashed guide line.
3. **Marking the Door Width:** From that guide line, use the **Tape Measure tool** again. Click the guide and drag further right, type `3'`, and press **Enter**.
4. **Cutting the Opening:** Now that you have your markers, select the **Line tool**. Click on the bottom edge at the first guide, then click on the bottom edge at the second guide. 

By using the guides first, you have ensured the door is exactly 3 feet wide and positioned exactly 2 feet from the corner, without having to guess or "eye-ball" the distance.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Lines and Faces:** The Line tool creates **Edges**; when edges form a closed loop, they create a **Face**.
*   **Axis Locking:** Use the **Arrow Keys** (Right, Left, Up) to force lines to stay on the Red, Green, or Blue axes.
*   **Precision Input:** Never click in the Measurements box. Type your dimensions while the tool is active and press **Enter**.
*   **Shape Logic:** Rectangles require two dimensions (width, height), while Circles and Polygons require a radius.
*   **Construction Guides:** Use the **Tape Measure tool** to create dashed guides for layout and alignment; these are not part of the final geometry.

modules.title: Transforming 2D into 3D
modules.content:
## The Magic of the Third Dimension

Imagine you have spent an hour meticulously drawing the floor plan of a tiny house. You have the perimeter walls, the placement of the doors, and the exact dimensions of the rooms. Right now, it looks like a blueprint—a flat, 2D drawing resting on the ground plane. 

But here is the secret of 3D modeling: in SketchUp, a 2D shape isn't just a drawing; it is a **Face**. A face is a closed surface bounded by lines. Once you have a face, you no longer have to "draw" the walls; you simply "pull" them into existence. This transition from a flat plane to a volumetric object is where your project stops being a sketch and starts becoming a model.

## Giving Shape Depth with Push/Pull

The **Push/Pull tool** is the most iconic feature of SketchUp. Its sole purpose is to take a flat face and extrude it—meaning it pushes or pulls the surface along a straight line to create volume.

### How to Use Push/Pull
1. Select the **Push/Pull tool** from the Large Tool Set (it looks like a square with an upward-pointing arrow).
2. Hover your cursor over a **Face**. You will see a small dotted line and a face-highlight indicating that the surface is selectable.
3. Click once to start the operation.
4. Move your mouse upward (to pull the face out) or downward (to push it in).
5. Click a second time to set the height.

### Precision Control with the VCB
While "eyeballing" the height is fine for rough drafts, professional models require accuracy. To create a wall of a specific height:
1. Start the Push/Pull operation and move the mouse in the desired direction.
2. Release the mouse button (do not click a second time yet).
3. Type the exact dimension into the **Value Control Box (VCB)**—for example, `9'` or `250cm`.
4. Press **Enter**.

### Pro Tips for Push/Pull
*   **Pushing Through:** If you push a face completely through another face of the same size, SketchUp will "punch a hole" through the object, deleting both faces. This is the fastest way to create a window or door opening.
*   **Repeating the Action:** If you have multiple faces to extrude to the same height, you don't need to type the measurement every time. After completing one Push/Pull operation, select the next face and **Double-Click**. SketchUp will automatically apply the exact same distance as the previous action.

## Creating Thickness with the Offset Tool

In the real world, walls aren't infinitely thin lines; they have thickness for structural support and insulation. If you simply pull up a 2D rectangle, you create a solid block. To create a room with hollow interiors, you need the **Offset tool**.

**Offset** creates a copy of the edges of a face, scaled inward or outward, while maintaining the original shape.

### Creating Walls in Three Steps
To transform a flat rectangle into a room with 6-inch walls:
1. Select the **Offset tool** from the Large Tool Set.
2. Click on the face of your rectangle.
3. Move your cursor inward. You will see a new, smaller rectangle forming inside the original.
4. Type `6"` into the **VCB** and press **Enter**.

You now have a "frame" (the walls) and a center face (the floor). Now, use the **Push/Pull tool** on the frame to lift the walls upward, leaving the center floor flat.

### Common Uses for Offset
*   **Window Frames:** Offset a window opening inward to create the casing.
*   **Picture Frames:** Offset a rectangle to create the border of a frame.
*   **Sidewalks:** Offset the perimeter of a building outward to create a walking path around the exterior.

## Extruding Along a Path with Follow Me

The Push/Pull tool only moves in straight lines. But what if you need to create a crown molding, a pipe, a curved railing, or a picture frame that wraps around a room? For this, you use the **Follow Me tool**.

**Follow Me** takes a 2D face (the profile) and slides it along a path (the guide) to create a complex 3D volume.

### The Anatomy of a Follow Me Operation
To use this tool, you need two distinct elements:
1. **The Path:** A line or a series of connected lines that define the route the shape will take.
2. **The Profile:** A 2D face that represents the "cross-section" of the object.

### Step-by-Step: Creating a Baseboard
Imagine you want to add a decorative baseboard to the bottom of your walls.
1. **Draw the Path:** Use the Line tool to draw the perimeter of the room on the floor.
2. **Draw the Profile:** At one corner of the room, draw a small vertical rectangle (e.g., 4 inches high and 1 inch thick) perpendicular to the path.
3. **Select the Path:** This is the most important step. Select the **Path** first using the Select tool (click the lines of the floor perimeter).
4. **Activate Follow Me:** Select the **Follow Me tool** from the Large Tool Set.
5. **Click the Profile:** Click the small rectangle you drew in step 2.

SketchUp will "sweep" that rectangle along the entire perimeter, creating a continuous baseboard.

### Troubleshooting Follow Me
If the shape looks twisted or "implodes," it is usually because the profile face was not perfectly perpendicular to the path. Ensure your profile is facing the direction of travel for the cleanest results.

## Modifying Faces for Complex Openings

Once you have a volumetric 3D form, you often need to carve into it. This is where you move from "adding" volume to "subtracting" it.

### Creating Doorways and Windows
To create a door in a wall you have already extruded:
1. Use the **Rectangle tool** to draw a door-shaped face directly on the surface of the wall.
2. Select the **Push/Pull tool**.
3. Click the door face and push it into the wall.
4. Watch the status bar or the face itself; push until the face meets the back surface of the wall.
5. When the face "snaps" and disappears, you have successfully created a void.

### Creating Slopes and Angles
You aren't limited to 90-degree angles. You can modify faces to create slanted roofs or angled architectural features.

**The "Cut" Method:**
1. Use the **Line tool** to draw a diagonal line across a face.
2. This splits one large face into two smaller faces.
3. Use **Push/Pull** on only one of those faces. 
4. By pushing one side in or pulling it out, you create a stepped or slanted effect.

### Creating "Tunnels" and Cut-outs
If you have a complex 3D object and need a hole to go through it at an angle, you can use a combination of the tools learned so far:
*   Draw a shape on the surface.
*   Use **Push/Pull** to create a "plug" that goes into the object.
*   If the hole needs to be curved, use **Follow Me** to push a profile through the object along a curved path.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Faces are the Foundation:** You cannot use 3D tools on a single line; you must have a closed **Face** to create volume.
*   **Push/Pull for Volume:** Use this tool to extrude faces into 3D shapes or to "punch" holes through objects.
*   **Offset for Thickness:** Use this to create concentric shapes, which is essential for creating walls, frames, and borders.
*   **Follow Me for Paths:** Use this to extrude a profile along a line to create moldings, pipes, or curved architectural elements.
*   **Order of Operations:** For the Follow Me tool, always select the **Path** first, then activate the tool, then click the **Profile**.
*   **Subtractive Modeling:** Creating openings (doors/windows) is done by pushing a face through the volume until it disappears.

modules.title: Editing and Modifying Geometry
modules.content:
## Mastering the Art of Shaping Your Model

Every great 3D model starts with a rough shape—but the magic happens in the editing. Think of your model like a block of clay. The initial sketch might capture the basic form, but it’s the careful pushing, pulling, twisting, and scaling that turns that lump into something recognizable. Whether you’re adjusting the height of a wall, fine-tuning the angle of a roof, or evening out the proportions of a chair, **editing and modifying geometry** is where precision meets creativity.

Imagine you’ve just drawn a simple box and extruded it into a cube. It’s a start—but now you need to make it a cabinet. You’ll want to stretch one side to create a door, tilt the top slightly to make a slanted lid, and maybe shrink the bottom to raise it off the ground. These aren’t new shapes; they’re refinements of the existing one. That’s what this chapter is about: **how to manipulate your geometry without redrawing everything**.

SketchUp gives you powerful tools to do this efficiently. You’ll learn to **move**, **rotate**, and **scale** objects with control. You’ll stretch edges to reshape faces, twist shapes along accurate axes, and resize parts of your model—all while keeping everything aligned and proportional. No prior experience is needed. By the end, you’ll be able to take a basic form and sculpt it into something precise, just like a digital sculptor.

Let’s begin.

---

## Moving Objects with Purpose

The **Move tool** is one of SketchUp’s most versatile. It does more than just shift objects from one place to another—it lets you **reshape** them by stretching edges and faces in real time. Whether you're nudging a window into a wall or pulling a wall upward to make a taller room, the Move tool gives you direct control over your model’s structure.

### Using the Move Tool

To activate the Move tool:
- Click the **Move** icon in the toolbar (it looks like four arrows pointing outward).
- Or press the **M** key on your keyboard.

Once selected, your cursor changes to a four-way arrow. Hover over any part of your model, and SketchUp highlights edges, faces, or vertices that can be moved.

### Moving Entire Objects

Let’s start simple. Suppose you’ve drawn a chair but placed it too close to a table. Select the Move tool, click once on the chair (this sets the **origin point**), then click again where you want the chair to go.

- Click to **pick up** the object
- Click to **place** it

This moves the entire object while keeping its shape intact.

> 💡 **Pro Tip:** Use **inference**—SketchUp’s way of guessing where you want to place something. Hover near edges or points to snap precisely.

### Stretching Edges and Faces

Now for the real power. The Move tool can **reshape** your geometry by pulling on edges or faces.

#### Stretching a Face

1. Select the Move tool (M).
2. Click on the face you want to stretch (e.g., the top of a table).
3. Move your cursor upward—SketchUp shows a preview of the stretched face.
4. Click to confirm the new height.

The face expands, and the surrounding geometry adjusts automatically. This is called **pushing/pulling**—a core concept in SketchUp.

#### Example: Making a Door

Imagine you’ve drawn a solid wall. To add a door:
1. Draw a rectangle on the wall face—this becomes the door opening.
2. Use the Move tool to click and drag the rectangle **into** the wall (this removes the material, creating an opening).
3. Now, select the door frame (the edges around the opening).
4. Use the Move tool to pull the top edge upward slightly—this creates a slight arch.
5. Finally, pull the bottom edge down to widen the base.

You’ve just reshaped your wall into a doorway with a curved top—all by moving edges.

> 🔍 **Jargon Alert:** A **face** is the flat surface inside an edge loop. An **edge** is a line connecting two points. A **vertex** is a corner point where edges meet.

### Moving Along an Axis

Sometimes you want to move only in one direction—like straight up, not diagonally. SketchUp helps with **axis locking**.

- After clicking to pick up an object or face, move your mouse in one direction (e.g., upward).
- Press the **Up Arrow** key to lock movement to the blue (Z) axis.
- Press the **Right Arrow** key to lock to the red (X) axis.
- Press the **Left Arrow** key to lock to the green (Y) axis.

This keeps your edits perfectly straight, avoiding unwanted diagonals.

### Common Move Tool Scenarios

| Scenario | How to Do It |
|--------|-------------|
| Lift a wall to make it taller | Select Move tool → Click top face → Drag upward → Click to confirm |
| Create a window in a wall | Draw a rectangle on the wall → Move tool → Click and drag inward to cut an opening |
| Adjust the slope of a roof | Select Move tool → Click the ridge edge → Drag upward to steepen the slope |
| Move a chair across the floor | Select Move tool → Click chair → Click new position |

---

## Rotating Objects with Precision

The **Rotate tool** lets you spin objects or parts of objects around a fixed point. Whether you're tilting a bookshelf to fit a corner, twisting a staircase railing, or angling a roof, rotation adds realism and functionality to your model.

### Using the Rotate Tool

Activate the Rotate tool:
- Click the **Rotate** icon (a curved arrow).
- Or press the **Q** key.

Your cursor changes to a rotation symbol. To rotate an object:
1. Click to set the **rotation center** (the pivot point).
2. Move your cursor to define the **rotation axis** (a blue line appears).
3. Drag to rotate.
4. Click to confirm.

### Setting the Pivot Point

The pivot point determines **where** the object rotates from. By default, it’s the center of the selected object, but you can change it.

- With the Rotate tool active, click once to set the pivot.
- Move your cursor and click again to set the direction of the rotation axis.

> 💡 **Tip:** To rotate around a specific vertex or edge, select it first with the Select tool, then activate the Rotate tool. The pivot will snap to that point.

### Using Guide Axes for Accurate Rotation

SketchUp uses **guide axes**—temporary blue, red, and green lines—to help you rotate along specific directions. When you start rotating, a blue axis appears. Press:
- **Up Arrow** to rotate around the blue (Z) axis
- **Right Arrow** to rotate around the red (X) axis
- **Left Arrow** to rotate around the green (Y) axis

This is especially useful for architectural elements like staircases or angled roofs.

#### Example: Creating a Spiral Staircase

1. Draw a circular base.
2. Use the Push/Pull tool to extrude it upward into a cylinder.
3. With the Rotate tool:
   - Click the center of the top face to set the pivot.
   - Press **Right Arrow** to lock rotation to the red axis.
   - Drag slightly to tilt one edge—this creates the start of the spiral.
4. Repeat with smaller rotations to build the staircase steps.

It’s not perfect, but it shows how rotation and repetition create complex shapes.

### Rotating Part of an Object

You can rotate just a section of your model—like a door on a hinge.

1. Select the door face.
2. Activate the Rotate tool.
3. Click the hinge edge (this sets the pivot along that edge).
4. Drag the door open.

The door swings around the hinge—no need to redraw it.

### Common Rotation Scenarios

| Scenario | How to Do It |
|--------|-------------|
| Open a door | Select door face → Rotate tool → Click hinge edge → Drag to swing |
| Tilt a monitor on a desk | Select monitor → Rotate tool → Click bottom edge → Tilt forward |
| Create a sloped roof | Select roof face → Rotate tool → Click base edge → Drag upward |
| Adjust a chair leg angle | Select leg → Rotate tool → Click top vertex → Rotate outward |

---

## Scaling Objects: From Tiny to Towering

The **Scale tool** resizes objects—making them larger, smaller, or even stretched unevenly. It’s essential when you need to match real-world dimensions or adjust proportions.

### Using the Scale Tool

Activate the Scale tool:
- Click the **Scale** icon (a square with arrows pointing outward).
- Or press the **S** key.

When selected, your object gets a bounding box with **scale handles** (small blue squares at corners and midpoints).

### Scaling Proportionally

To resize an object while keeping its shape intact:
1. Select the object.
2. Activate the Scale tool.
3. Click and drag one of the corner handles.
4. Move your cursor inward to shrink, outward to enlarge.
5. Click to confirm.

All dimensions change equally—height, width, and depth stay in proportion.

#### Example: Resizing a Chair

You’ve drawn a chair that’s too small. Select it, activate the Scale tool, and drag a corner handle outward. As you move, SketchUp shows a percentage change (e.g., 150% = 1.5x size). Release when it looks right.

### Scaling Non-Proportionally

Sometimes you want to stretch an object—like making a table longer but keeping the height the same.

1. Activate the Scale tool.
2. Click a **midpoint handle** (not a corner).
3. Drag outward along one axis only.

This stretches the object in one direction while keeping others fixed.

> ⚠️ **Caution:** Non-proportional scaling can distort your model. Use it sparingly.

### Scaling Along an Axis

Like the Move and Rotate tools, you can lock scaling to one axis:
- After activating the Scale tool, press:
  - **Up Arrow** to scale along the blue (Z) axis
  - **Right Arrow** to scale along the red (X) axis
  - **Left Arrow** to scale along the green (Y) axis

This is useful for resizing windows, doors, or furniture parts without affecting other dimensions.

### Scaling from a Fixed Point

By default, scaling happens from the object’s center. But you can change the **scale origin**:
- Click a point inside the bounding box before dragging a handle.
- This sets the pivot for scaling.

For example, to make a table grow from one leg:
1. Activate Scale tool.
2. Click near the bottom-left corner of the table.
3. Drag the opposite corner upward.

The table stretches from the selected point.

### Common Scaling Scenarios

| Scenario | How to Do It |
|--------|-------------|
| Make a chair taller | Select chair → Scale tool → Drag top midpoint upward |
| Widen a door frame | Select door → Scale tool → Drag side midpoint outward |
| Shrink a window | Select window → Scale tool → Drag corner inward to 80% |
| Stretch a bench seat | Select seat → Scale tool → Drag front midpoint forward |

---

## Putting It All Together: A Real-World Project

Let’s apply these tools in a practical example: designing a simple bookshelf.

### Step 1: Draw the Base
1. Use the Rectangle tool to draw a 1-meter-wide, 0.2-meter-deep base.
2. Push/Pull it upward to 1.8 meters tall.

### Step 2: Add Shelves
1. Draw a rectangle on the front face at 0.4 meters from the bottom.
2. Use the Move tool to pull it **into** the shelf (this cuts an opening).
3. Use Push/Pull to extrude the opening inward slightly—this becomes the shelf depth.
4. Repeat at 0.8m and 1.2m heights.

### Step 3: Adjust the Top
1. Select the top face.
2. Use the Move tool to lift it upward by 0.1 meters—this adds a slight overhang.
3. Now, use the Rotate tool to tilt the top face slightly backward (about 5 degrees) for a modern look.

### Step 4: Fine-Tune the Width
1. The shelf is too wide. Select the entire bookshelf.
2. Activate the Scale tool.
3. Drag the left midpoint handle inward to 0.9 meters.

### Result
You now have a 0.9m-wide, 1.8m-tall bookshelf with three adjustable shelves and a tilted top—all created by moving, rotating, and scaling.

---

## Tips for Smooth Editing

- **Work in small increments.** Small changes are easier to undo and adjust.
- **Use the Eraser tool** to clean up stray edges after moving or rotating.
- **Zoom in** when precision matters—use the Scroll Wheel or Camera > Zoom Extents.
- **Undo often.** SketchUp’s undo (Ctrl/Cmd + Z) is your best friend.
- **Use inference**—Snapping to edges, midpoints, and intersections keeps everything aligned.

---

## Key Takeaways

- The **Move tool** lets you shift objects and **reshape geometry** by stretching faces and edges. Use axis locking (arrow keys) for precision.
- The **Rotate tool** spins objects around a pivot. Set the pivot point by clicking during rotation, and use guide axes (arrow keys) to control the rotation axis.
- The **Scale tool** resizes objects **proportionally** (corner handles) or **non-proportionally** (midpoint handles). Lock scaling to one axis with arrow keys.
- All three tools work with **inference**, allowing you to snap to edges, faces, and vertices for accurate placement.
- Always **test small changes**, use **undo frequently**, and **zoom in** when detail matters.
- Editing geometry is about **refinement**, not redrawing—every adjustment brings your model closer to reality.

Now that you can shape and reshape your models, your next step is to organize them into reusable parts. But that’s for the next chapter. For now, practice moving, rotating, and scaling—your models will thank you.

modules.title: Organizing with Groups and Components
modules.content:
## Why Your Model is a Mess (and How to Fix It)

Imagine this: you’ve spent hours meticulously building a detailed kitchen model in SketchUp—cabinets, countertops, even a fridge with perfectly placed handles. Then, you try to move the fridge. Suddenly, the entire countertop glues itself to the fridge like it’s magnetized. Or worse, you accidentally edit one cabinet door, and suddenly *all* of them change because they were all just copies of the same piece. Frustrating, right?

This is what happens when you don’t organize your model properly. SketchUp doesn’t automatically keep your geometry separate—it treats everything as one big, connected blob unless you tell it otherwise. That’s where **groups** and **components** come in. They’re like invisible containers that keep your model’s pieces from sticking together and allow you to reuse assets without repeating work.

By the end of this chapter, you’ll know how to:
- Keep different parts of your model from interfering with each other
- Reuse objects (like doors or windows) without duplicating geometry
- Edit multiple copies of the same object all at once
- Navigate and manage complex models with ease

Let’s fix that messy kitchen—starting now.

---

## Groups: Your First Line of Defense

A **group** is a simple container that isolates a set of geometry from the rest of your model. Think of it like putting a lid on a jar: what’s inside stays separate from what’s outside. This prevents accidental edits and keeps geometry from merging when you don’t want it to.

### When to Use Groups

Use groups for:
- **Single objects** that should move or rotate as a unit (e.g., a chair, a lamp, a potted plant)
- **Small assemblies** that you might need to edit later without affecting the whole model (e.g., a drawer with multiple parts)
- **Temporary isolation** while you work on a specific part of your model

Groups are perfect when you’re still figuring out your design and need flexibility. They’re lightweight and easy to create.

### How to Create a Group

1. **Select the geometry** you want to group. This could be a single shape, multiple edges, or even an entire complex object.
2. **Right-click** on the selection.
3. Choose **Make Group** from the context menu.

That’s it. Your geometry is now wrapped in an invisible box.

**Pro Tip:** You can also use the shortcut **Ctrl+G** (Windows) or **Cmd+G** (Mac) after making your selection. Memorizing this will save you time.

### Editing a Group

Here’s where groups get powerful. To edit what’s inside a group without affecting the rest of your model:

1. **Double-click** on the group.
   - The rest of the model will dim slightly, and the group’s edges will highlight in blue.
   - You’re now *inside* the group, editing its contents.
2. Make your changes (move, resize, delete, etc.).
3. **Click outside the group** or press **Esc** to exit.

**Notice how the rest of your model stays untouched?** That’s the magic of groups.

### Ungrouping

If you need to break a group apart (e.g., you realize the grouping was a mistake), select the group and right-click, then choose **Explode**. The group’s geometry returns to the main model as separate edges and faces.

**Warning:** Exploding a group turns it back into raw geometry. If you had nested groups inside it, they’ll also explode, potentially creating a mess. Use this sparingly.

---

## Components: Reusable Assets

Groups are great for isolation, but they have a limitation: if you copy a group and edit one instance, the others won’t update. That’s where **components** come in. A component is like a group, but with a superpower—**changes to one instance automatically update all the others**.

### Why Components Matter

Imagine modeling a row of identical chairs for a dining table. With groups, if you decide to add armrests to one chair, you’d have to edit each group individually. With components, you edit one chair, and *all* the chairs update instantly.

Components are essential for:
- **Reusable objects** (doors, windows, furniture)
- **Large-scale repetition** (flooring, tiles, balusters)
- **Efficient editing** (one change, many updates)

### Creating a Component

1. **Select the geometry** you want to turn into a component.
2. Right-click and choose **Make Component** (or press **Ctrl+Alt+G** / **Cmd+Option+G**).
3. In the dialog box:
   - Give your component a **name** (e.g., "Chair Wooden Armchair").
   - Choose a **definition** (more on this below).
   - Set **glue to** if needed (we’ll cover this later).
4. Click **Create**.

**Definition?** Think of it as a blueprint. All instances of this component share the same definition. Changing the definition updates every instance.

### Editing a Component

There are two ways to edit a component:

#### 1. Editing the Definition (Affects All Instances)
1. **Right-click** on any instance of the component.
2. Choose **Edit Component**.
3. Make your changes. All other instances will update automatically.
4. **Click outside** or press **Esc** to exit.

#### 2. Editing a Single Instance (Without Affecting Others)
If you want to tweak one instance without changing the others:
1. **Right-click** on the instance.
2. Choose **Make Unique** (this creates a one-off copy with its own definition).
3. Now you can edit this instance freely—it won’t affect the others.

**Example:** You have 10 identical chairs, but one needs a scratch. Make it unique, edit the scratch, and the rest stay pristine.

### Managing Components with the Outliner

As your model grows, keeping track of groups and components can get overwhelming. The **Outliner** is your lifesaver.

To open the Outliner:
- Go to **Window > Outliner** (or press **Ctrl+Shift+O** / **Cmd+Shift+O**).

The Outliner shows a **hierarchy** of your model’s organization, like a family tree:
- **Main Model** (the root)
  - **Group 1**
    - **Component A**
    - **Group 2**
  - **Component B**

**Why hierarchy matters:**
- Click an item in the Outliner to **select it** in the viewport.
- Drag items to **reorganize** them (e.g., move a group inside another group).
- Collapse/expand branches to **simplify the view**.

**Pro Tip:** Rename items in the Outliner by double-clicking their names. Descriptive names (e.g., "Front Door" instead of "Component1") make your life easier later.

---

## Nested Groups and Components

Complex models often require **nesting**—putting groups or components inside other groups or components. For example, a bookshelf might be a component, but its individual shelves could be groups inside it.

### Why Nesting Helps

- **Organization:** Break a complex model into logical parts.
- **Performance:** Smaller, isolated pieces are easier for SketchUp to handle.
- **Editing:** Isolate specific parts without affecting the whole.

### How to Nest

1. Create your inner group/component first (e.g., a single shelf).
2. Select it and **Make Group** or **Make Component**.
3. Now select that group/component along with other geometry (e.g., side panels).
4. **Make Group** or **Make Component** again to nest it inside a larger assembly.

**Example:** Building a chair
- Create the seat as a group.
- Create the backrest as a separate group.
- Select both and make a "Chair" component. Now the chair is a single unit, but its parts are still editable.

### Editing Nested Items

To edit something deep inside a hierarchy:
1. Double-click the outer group/component to enter it.
2. Double-click the inner group/component to enter *that*.
3. Make your changes.
4. Click outside twice (or press **Esc** twice) to return to the main model.

**Shortcut:** Use the **Selection Tool (Spacebar)** and **double-click** to drill down into nested items.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Even with groups and components, it’s easy to run into issues. Here’s how to sidestep them:

### 1. Accidental Grouping/Component Creation
- **Problem:** You meant to select one chair but accidentally grouped the whole row.
- **Fix:** Use **Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z)** to undo immediately. Or, before grouping, hide (**View > Hidden Geometry**) or lock (**Window > Model Info > Components**) parts you don’t want to include.

### 2. Components Updating When You Don’t Want Them To
- **Problem:** You edit one instance of a component, expecting only that one to change, but all instances update.
- **Fix:** Remember to **Make Unique** if you want to edit a single instance without affecting others.

### 3. Geometry "Sticking" Together
- **Problem:** Two groups/components merge when you move them close together.
- **Fix:** This usually happens when geometry overlaps. Use **Outliner** to check for hidden edges or faces. Alternatively, add a small gap between objects.

### 4. Outliner Becoming a Jungle
- **Problem:** Your Outliner is a mess of "Group1," "Component2," etc.
- **Fix:** Rename items as you go. Delete unused groups/components (right-click > **Delete**). Use folders (click the **+** in the Outliner) to group related items.

### 5. Performance Slowdowns
- **Problem:** Your model lags when you zoom in or out.
- **Fix:** Avoid nesting too deeply. Groups/components inside groups/components can slow things down. Keep your hierarchy shallow where possible.

---

## A Real-World Workflow: Building a Bookshelf

Let’s apply what you’ve learned to a practical example—building a simple bookshelf.

### Step 1: Plan Your Assembly
A bookshelf has:
- A top and bottom shelf (similar)
- Two side panels (identical)
- Shelves in between (repeated)
- Optional back panel

### Step 2: Create Individual Parts
1. **Side Panels:**
   - Draw a rectangle (use the **Rectangle Tool** from the **Large Tool Set**).
   - Push/Pull to 3D (use the **Push/Pull Tool**).
   - Select the panel and **Make Component** (name it "Bookshelf Side Panel").
2. **Shelves:**
   - Draw another rectangle (same width as the side panels, shallower depth).
   - Push/Pull to thickness.
   - **Make Component** (name it "Bookshelf Shelf").
3. **Top/Bottom:**
   - Repeat the shelf process but make these slightly wider if needed.
   - **Make Component** (name it "Bookshelf Top/Bottom").

### Step 3: Assemble the Bookshelf
1. Place two **Side Panels** parallel to each other.
2. Add a **Top/Bottom** component at the top and bottom.
3. Add **Shelf** components in between.
4. Adjust spacing as needed.

**Why components?** If you decide to change the shelf thickness later, edit the "Bookshelf Shelf" component, and every shelf updates automatically.

### Step 4: Add a Back Panel (Optional)
1. Draw a thin rectangle covering the back.
2. **Make Group** (since it’s a single piece and won’t be reused).
3. Position it behind the shelves.

### Step 5: Test Your Model
- Try moving one shelf. Does it stay in place? If not, check if it’s grouped/comp grouped correctly.
- Use the **Outliner** to verify your hierarchy.

---

## Advanced Tips for Power Users

Once you’re comfortable with basics, try these:

### Gluing Components
Some components can "glue" to other geometry to simplify placement. For example:
1. Create a door component with "Glue to" set to **Face** in the component options.
2. When you move the door near a wall, it will snap to the wall’s face.

**How to set glue:**
- When creating the component, in the dialog box, set **glue to** to the appropriate option (e.g., **Face** or **Ceiling**).

### Component Options
Components can have customizable parameters. For example:
- A window component with options for width, height, and pane count.
- To set this up, you’ll need to use **Dynamic Components** (an extension), but it’s a powerful tool for reusable, adjustable objects.

### Libraries and Repositories
Save your components to reuse in future projects:
1. Right-click a component in the Outliner.
2. Choose **Save As...** to export it as a `.skp` file.
3. In new models, use **File > 3D Warehouse > Get Models** or **File > Import** to bring it in.

---
## Key Takeaways

- **Groups** isolate geometry to prevent accidental edits and merging. Use them for single objects or temporary isolation.
- **Components** are groups with superpowers: edit one instance, and all others update automatically. Use them for reusable assets.
- **Nesting** lets you build complex models by combining groups/components. Edit nested items by double-clicking through the hierarchy.
- The **Outliner** is your best friend for navigating and managing your model’s organization. Rename items and collapse branches to stay sane.
- Avoid common pitfalls like accidental grouping, nested chaos, and performance slowdowns by planning your hierarchy and cleaning up as you go.
- Start simple: group first, then convert frequently reused items to components as your model grows.

With groups and components, your models will stay organized, your edits will be efficient, and your sanity will remain intact. Now go build something messy—and then fix it properly.

modules.title: Applying Materials and Textures
modules.content:
## What’s the First Thing You Notice in a 3D Model?

When you walk into a furnished room, the colors, fabrics, and finishes are usually the first things that catch your eye. A shiny marble countertop, a rough brick wall, or the soft sheen of a wooden table—these surfaces tell a story about the space. In SketchUp, you’re not just building empty boxes; you’re crafting environments where materials and textures bring your design to life. Without them, your model is just a collection of lines and shapes floating in space.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to add realism to your models by applying materials—whether it’s the default brick texture on a wall, a custom wood grain for your furniture, or a carefully placed image as a floor pattern. You’ll also discover how to adjust textures so they look natural on your surfaces, not stretched or misaligned. By the end, you’ll have the skills to turn your 3D sketches into something that looks like it could exist in the real world.

---

## Meet the Paint Bucket: Your First Step to Realism

The **Paint Bucket** tool is your gateway to applying materials in SketchUp. It works just like a real paint bucket—you select a material (or "paint") and then "paint" it onto the surfaces of your model. This tool is found in the **Default Tray** under the **Materials** panel, or you can quickly access it by pressing the **B** key on your keyboard.

### How to Use the Paint Bucket
1. **Open the Materials Panel**
   - If the Materials panel isn’t already visible, go to **Window > Materials** to open it.
   - The panel will display a grid of default materials, organized into categories like **Concrete**, **Wood**, **Metal**, and **Colors**.

2. **Select a Material**
   - Click on any material thumbnail to select it. The selected material will appear in the preview box at the top of the panel.
   - Hover over a material to see its name (e.g., "Brick - Red" or "Wood - Oak").

3. **Apply the Material**
   - With the Paint Bucket tool active (or by pressing **B**), click on any surface in your model to apply the selected material.
   - If you click on a surface that already has a material, it will be replaced with the new one.

### Real-World Analogy
Think of the Paint Bucket like a physical paint can. You wouldn’t pour the entire can onto a wall—you’d dip a brush (or roller) and apply it to the surface. The Paint Bucket in SketchUp is the same: select your "paint," then apply it to the surfaces you want to color.

---

## Default Materials: Quick and Easy Styling

SketchUp comes with a library of **default materials** that cover common surfaces like wood, metal, brick, and glass. These are perfect for getting started because they’re ready to use—no extra steps required.

### Categories of Default Materials
The Materials panel organizes materials into these key categories:
- **Concrete**: Smooth, rough, or patterned textures for floors, walls, and sidewalks.
- **Wood**: Planks, beams, and panels in various species like oak, pine, or mahogany.
- **Metal**: Shiny or brushed finishes for appliances, railings, or industrial details.
- **Brick**: Red, brown, or white bricks with realistic mortar lines.
- **Glass**: Transparent or frosted textures for windows and doors.
- **Colors**: Solid colors (like red, blue, or gray) for quick accents or backgrounds.

### Applying a Default Material
Let’s say you’ve drawn a simple house and want to give it a wooden exterior:
1. Open the Materials panel (**Window > Materials**).
2. Click the **Wood** category.
3. Scroll through the thumbnails to find a wood texture you like (e.g., "Wood - Cedar").
4. Click on the thumbnail to select it.
5. With the Paint Bucket tool active (press **B**), click on the walls of your house to apply the wood texture.

**Pro Tip:** If the texture looks too large or too small, don’t worry—we’ll fix that later with the Texture tool.

---

## Custom Textures: Bringing Your Own Images to Life

Default materials are great for quick results, but sometimes you need a specific texture—like a photo of a rare marble slab or a custom fabric for a sofa. SketchUp lets you import your own images as textures, which you can then apply to any surface.

### Supported Image Formats
SketchUp supports common image formats like:
- **JPEG (.jpg)**
- **PNG (.png)**
- **TIFF (.tif)**
- **BMP (.bmp)**

### How to Import a Custom Texture
1. **Prepare Your Image**
   - Your image should be high-resolution enough for your model’s scale. For example, if you’re applying a texture to a 10-foot wall, a 1024x768 image might look blurry. Aim for at least 2048x2048 pixels for large surfaces.
   - Save the image in a folder you can easily access.

2. **Create a Custom Material**
   - Open the Materials panel (**Window > Materials**).
   - Click the **Create Material** button (it looks like a blank page with a + sign).
   - In the dialog box that appears:
     - Give your material a **Name** (e.g., "Custom Marble").
     - Click the **Browse** button to select your image file.
     - Click **OK** to create the material.

3. **Apply the Custom Texture**
   - Your new material will appear in the Materials panel. Select it by clicking on its thumbnail.
   - Use the Paint Bucket tool (**B**) to click on any surface in your model to apply the texture.

### Example: Adding a Custom Floor Pattern
Imagine you’re designing a kitchen and want to use a specific tile pattern you found online:
1. Save the tile image to your desktop.
2. Open the Materials panel and click **Create Material**.
3. Name it "Kitchen Tile" and browse to select the image.
4. Apply the texture to the floor surface in your model.

**Troubleshooting:**
- If the texture doesn’t look right, it might be too small. We’ll adjust the scale next.
- If the image appears distorted, it could be because the surface you’re applying it to is not flat. Use the **Rectangle** or **Push/Pull** tools to ensure your surface is a flat plane before applying textures.

---

## Adjusting Texture Scale and Position: Making Textures Look Natural

One of the most common mistakes beginners make is applying a texture that looks stretched, squashed, or misaligned. For example, a brick texture might appear too large on a small wall, or a wood grain might run vertically when you want it horizontal. The **Texture** tool (also called the **Position** tool) lets you fix these issues.

### The Texture Tool Explained
The Texture tool allows you to:
- **Scale** the texture to the right size.
- **Rotate** the texture to align it properly.
- **Move** the texture within the surface.

### How to Adjust a Texture
1. **Select the Surface**
   - Use the **Select** tool (**Spacebar**) to click on the surface with the texture you want to adjust.

2. **Activate the Texture Tool**
   - Press **T** on your keyboard to activate the Texture tool.
   - Alternatively, go to **Tools > Texture > Position**.

3. **Adjust the Texture**
   - **Scale:** Click and drag one of the green handles (squares) at the corners of the texture to make it larger or smaller.
   - **Rotate:** Click and drag the circular handle in the center to rotate the texture.
   - **Move:** Click and drag the texture itself (not the handles) to reposition it within the surface.

### Example: Fixing a Brick Wall
You’ve applied a brick texture to a wall, but it looks too large:
1. Select the wall.
2. Press **T** to activate the Texture tool.
3. Click and drag one of the corner handles inward to shrink the brick pattern until it looks natural.
4. If the bricks are running horizontally but you want them vertical, drag the circular handle to rotate the texture.

**Pro Tip:** Hold the **Shift** key while dragging to constrain the scaling or rotation to perfect 90-degree angles.

---

## Creating and Saving a Custom Material Library

As you work on projects, you’ll likely accumulate a collection of custom materials—textures for fabrics, unique wallpapers, or specialized flooring. Instead of recreating these materials every time you start a new model, you can save them in a **custom material library** for easy access.

### How to Create a Custom Material Library
1. **Open the Materials Panel**
   - Go to **Window > Materials**.

2. **Create a New Library**
   - Click the **Materials** dropdown menu in the top-right corner of the panel.
   - Select **New Material Library**.
   - Name your library (e.g., "My Custom Textures") and save it to a location on your computer (e.g., your SketchUp folder).

3. **Add Materials to the Library**
   - Open the default Materials panel by clicking the **Materials** dropdown and selecting **In Model** or another category.
   - Drag and drop materials from the default panel into your new library.
   - To add custom materials, use the **Create Material** button and save them directly to your library.

4. **Save the Library**
   - Your library is automatically saved when you close SketchUp. To share it with others or back it up, you can export it:
     - Click the **Materials** dropdown and select **Save As**.
     - Choose a location and name for your library file (.skm or .skp format).

### Example: Building a Kitchen Materials Library
You’re designing a kitchen and want to keep all your cabinet, countertop, and backsplash materials in one place:
1. Create a new library called "Kitchen Textures."
2. Add default materials like "Wood - Maple" for cabinets and "Granite - Black" for countertops.
3. Import custom images for unique backsplash tiles.
4. Save the library so you can reuse it in future kitchen projects.

**Why Use a Custom Library?**
- **Consistency:** Keep the same materials across multiple projects.
- **Efficiency:** Avoid recreating textures from scratch.
- **Organization:** Group related materials together (e.g., all flooring textures in one library).

---

## Putting It All Together: A Real-World Scenario

Let’s walk through a complete example to tie everything together. Imagine you’re designing a small café:

1. **Model the Space**
   - You’ve already drawn the walls, floor, and furniture using the tools from previous chapters.

2. **Apply Default Materials**
   - Use the Paint Bucket to apply:
     - **Concrete - Smooth** to the floor.
     - **Wood - Oak** to the counter and tables.
     - **Brick - Red** to the accent wall.

3. **Import a Custom Texture**
   - Find an image of a coffee bean sack online and save it to your computer.
   - Create a new material named "Coffee Bean Sack" and import the image.
   - Apply the texture to one wall as a decorative element.

4. **Adjust the Texture**
   - The coffee bean sack looks too large, so select the wall and press **T** to adjust the scale.
   - Rotate the texture slightly so the beans run horizontally.

5. **Create a Material Library**
   - Save all the textures you’ve used (concrete, wood, brick, coffee sack) into a library called "Café Textures."
   - Next time you design a café, you can reuse these materials instantly.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Even with these tools, beginners often run into issues when applying materials. Here’s how to troubleshoot the most common problems:

### 1. Textures Look Blurry or Pixelated
- **Cause:** The image resolution is too low for the surface size.
- **Fix:** Use a higher-resolution image or scale the texture down in the Texture tool.

### 2. Textures Won’t Apply
- **Cause:** The surface isn’t a flat plane (e.g., it’s a curved or non-rectangular face).
- **Fix:** Use the **Rectangle** or **Push/Pull** tools to ensure the surface is flat and rectangular before applying textures.

### 3. Textures Look Stretched
- **Cause:** The surface is longer in one direction than the other (e.g., a very long wall with a square brick pattern).
- **Fix:** Use the Texture tool to scale the texture unevenly by dragging only the horizontal or vertical handles.

### 4. Materials Disappear When Saved
- **Cause:** The material was only applied to the model in memory and wasn’t saved to the material library.
- **Fix:** Always save custom materials to a library or export your model as a .skp file, which preserves the materials.

---

## Key Takeaways

- The **Paint Bucket tool** is your primary way to apply materials in SketchUp. Press **B** to activate it and click surfaces to add color and texture.
- **Default materials** provide quick, realistic options for common surfaces like wood, brick, and metal. Use the Materials panel to browse and apply them.
- To use your own images as textures, **create a custom material** by importing the image into the Materials panel. This is useful for unique surfaces like fabrics or custom tiles.
- The **Texture tool** (press **T**) lets you **scale, rotate, and reposition** textures to make them look natural on your surfaces. Avoid stretched or misaligned textures by adjusting them carefully.
- **Custom material libraries** help you organize and reuse textures across projects. Save your favorite materials into a library for future use.
- Always check that your surfaces are **flat and rectangular** before applying textures, or the material won’t look correct.
- If a texture looks blurry or pixelated, it’s likely because the image resolution is too low for the surface size. Use higher-resolution images or scale the texture down.

modules.title: Using Tags and Scenes
modules.content:
## Why Visibility Matters in Your SketchUp Model

Imagine you're working on a two-story house in SketchUp. You've spent hours modeling the walls, doors, windows, furniture, and landscaping. Now, you want to show the client just the exterior view—but when you zoom out, the interior furniture, plumbing lines, and electrical conduits are cluttering your view. Every time you orbit, elements you don’t need right now are slowing down your workflow and distracting your focus.

This is where **Tags** and **Scenes** become essential. Tags help you organize and control what’s visible. Scenes let you save specific camera angles and visibility settings so you can instantly jump to exactly the view you want—whether you're presenting to a client, collaborating with a team, or just trying to work efficiently.

By the end of this chapter, you'll know how to keep your models tidy, your navigation smooth, and your presentations sharp—without ever losing track of your work.

---

## Working with Tags: Your Model’s Organizational Backbone

### What Are Tags?

In SketchUp, **Tags** (formerly called *Layers*) are like digital folders that help you group and control the visibility of different parts of your model. Think of them as color-coded tabs in a binder:

- **Wall** → All exterior and interior walls
- **Doors** → All doors
- **Windows** → All windows
- **Furniture** → Sofas, tables, chairs
- **Electrical** → Wiring, outlets, switches
- **Landscape** → Trees, bushes, paving

Each object in your model can be assigned to one or more Tags. This doesn't affect the geometry—it only controls whether that object appears in your view or not.

> 🔍 *Pro Tip:* Tags are about **visibility**, not organization of geometry. Objects can still be grouped or made into components even when assigned to Tags. Tags are purely for display control.

---

### Creating and Managing Tags

Let’s walk through how to create and use Tags in your model.

#### Step 1: Open the Tags Panel
1. Go to **Window > Tags** (on Windows) or **View > Tags Panel** (on Mac).
2. The **Tags panel** appears—usually on the right side of your screen.

#### Step 2: Add a New Tag
1. Click the **+** (plus) icon at the top of the Tags panel.
2. Name your new Tag: type `Walls` and press **Enter**.
3. Repeat to create `Doors`, `Windows`, and `Furniture`.

> 💡 *Best Practice:* Use clear, consistent names. Avoid spaces and special characters (e.g., use `Electrical` instead of `Elect. & Plumbing`). This makes filtering and scripting easier later.

#### Step 3: Assign Objects to Tags

Now, assign parts of your model to the appropriate Tags:

1. Select the walls in your model.
2. In the Tags panel, click the checkbox next to `Walls`. It will turn blue, indicating the selection is now part of the Walls Tag.
3. Repeat for doors, windows, and furniture.

> ⚠️ Important: You’ll see a warning: *"Adding entities to tags is deprecated."* This is a legacy message. In modern SketchUp (2020 and later), assigning objects to Tags is still the correct way to control visibility—even though the message might seem confusing. Ignore the warning.

---

### Controlling Visibility with Tags

Now that your objects are tagged, you can control what’s visible:

1. In the Tags panel, **uncheck** the box next to `Doors`.
2. All doors disappear from your model view.
3. Check it again—they reappear instantly.

This is **non-destructive visibility control**—your geometry is still there, but you’re choosing not to see it right now.

> ✅ *Use Case:* When modeling the roof, turn off `Furniture`, `Electrical`, and `Landscape`. Your screen stays clean, and SketchUp runs faster because it’s not rendering unnecessary geometry.

---

### Best Practices for Tagging

- **Tag by Function, Not Geometry Type**: Instead of `Lines` or `Curves`, use `Foundation`, `Roof`, `Stairs`.
- **Keep It Simple**: Start with 5–10 Tags. Too many Tags can be harder to manage.
- **Use Color Coding (Optional)**: While SketchUp doesn’t enforce color, you can assign colors to Tags in some extensions. This helps visually distinguish them in the panel.
- **Tag Early and Often**: Add Tags as you model, not after. It’s easier to assign as you go.

---

## Using the Outliner for Navigation

As your model grows, so does the number of objects. The **Outliner** becomes your best friend.

1. Go to **Window > Outliner**.
2. The Outliner shows a list of all Groups, Components, and Tags in your model.
3. You can expand Tags to see what’s inside them.
4. Double-click an item to select it in the model.

> 🔎 *Pro Tip:* Use the Outliner to quickly find and isolate parts of your model. Combine it with Tags to zoom straight to the walls or furniture.

---

## Creating Scenes: Saving Your Views for Later

Now that your model is organized, how do you save specific views? That’s where **Scenes** come in.

### What Is a Scene?

A **Scene** is a saved snapshot of your model that includes:

- The camera angle (position and direction)
- Visible Tags
- Section planes
- Shadow settings (if enabled)
- Style settings

Scenes are perfect for presentations. Instead of manually orbiting and zooming every time, you click a Scene and—*whoosh*—you’re there.

---

### Creating Your First Scene

Let’s say you want to save a view of the exterior of your house.

1. **Set Up Your View:**
   - Use **Orbit** and **Pan** to position the camera at a standard exterior angle (e.g., slightly above and in front of the house).
   - Use **Zoom** to frame the house nicely in the viewport.

2. **Adjust Visibility:**
   - In the Tags panel, make sure only `Walls`, `Doors`, `Windows`, and `Roof` are visible. Turn off `Furniture`, `Electrical`, and `Landscape`.

3. **Save the Scene:**
   - Go to **Window > Scenes**.
   - Click the **+** (plus) icon at the top of the Scenes panel.
   - Name it `Exterior View` and press **Enter**.

> ✅ *Save Often:* After each major modeling session, save a Scene. It only takes a second and prevents losing your work.

---

### Editing and Updating Scenes

What if you want to tweak the view after saving?

1. Adjust your camera angle or Tag visibility.
2. In the Scenes panel, right-click the `Exterior View` scene.
3. Choose **Update Scene**.
4. The scene now reflects your new settings.

> 🔄 *Use Update Cautiously:* Updating overwrites the previous version. If you want to keep both, create a new Scene instead (e.g., `Exterior View v2`).

---

### Organizing Scenes for Presentations

As your project grows, you’ll have multiple Scenes:

- `Exterior Day`
- `Exterior Night`
- `Floor Plan`
- `Interior Living Room`
- `Interior Kitchen`

To keep them organized:

1. In the Scenes panel, drag and drop to reorder them.
2. Use **Add Scene** to create new ones.
3. Use **Delete** (right-click) to remove unused Scenes.

> 📌 *Presentation Flow:* Arrange Scenes in the order you want to present them. This makes client meetings smoother.

---

## Managing Performance with Visibility

Large SketchUp models can slow down when too many objects are visible. Tags and Scenes help improve performance:

- **Hide Complex Elements:** Turn off `Furniture` or `Electrical` when modeling the roof.
- **Use Scenes for Rendering:** When exporting or rendering, use a Scene that hides unnecessary Tags to speed up the process.
- **Limit Real-Time Rendering:** SketchUp only renders what’s visible. Fewer visible objects = faster navigation.

> 🐢 *Performance Tip:* If SketchUp feels sluggish, try:
> 1. Hide Tags with many objects.
> 2. Use **Camera > Zoom Extents** to reset your view.
> 3. Check for large, ungrouped geometry.

---

## A Real-World Workflow: Modeling a Kitchen

Let’s walk through a practical example.

**Scenario:** You're modeling a kitchen with cabinets, appliances, countertops, and flooring.

1. **Tag the Model:**
   - `Walls`
   - `Cabinets`
   - `Appliances`
   - `Countertops`
   - `Flooring`
   - `Electrical`

2. **Model in Stages:**
   - Start with `Walls` visible.
   - Add `Cabinets` and model them.
   - Toggle `Electrical` on to place outlets.
   - Turn off `Electrical` when modeling countertops.

3. **Create Scenes:**
   - `Kitchen Layout` → Top-down view, all Tags visible.
   - `Cabinet Detail` → Zoomed-in view of a single cabinet.
   - `Appliance Placement` → Showing fridge, stove, sink.
   - `Final Render` → Clean view, only `Walls`, `Cabinets`, and `Appliances`.

4. **Present to Client:**
   - Click through Scenes in order.
   - Explain the layout, then zoom into details.
   - End with the final render view.

> ✅ *Client-Friendly:* Clients love clear, focused views. Scenes make you look professional and prepared.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

### Issue: Objects Disappeared and I Don’t Know Why
- **Check:** Are their Tags unchecked?
- **Fix:** Go to the Tags panel and make sure the correct Tags are visible.

### Issue: Scene doesn’t look right
- **Check:** Did you update it after changing the view?
- **Fix:** Right-click the scene and choose **Update Scene**.

### Issue: Tags panel is messy
- **Fix:** Delete unused Tags. Use the **–** (minus) icon to remove them.

### Issue: Model is slow
- **Fix:** Hide unnecessary Tags. Use Scenes to control what’s visible during modeling.

---

## Putting It All Together

Here’s a quick checklist to apply what you’ve learned:

✅ Create Tags for major elements in your model
✅ Assign objects to Tags as you model
✅ Use the Tags panel to toggle visibility
✅ Open the Outliner to navigate complex models
✅ Set up your camera angle and visibility
✅ Save a Scene
✅ Repeat for key views
✅ Organize Scenes in the Scenes panel
✅ Use Scenes during presentations or modeling

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Tags** are for **visibility control**, not geometry organization. They let you show or hide groups of objects instantly.
- Use **clear, consistent naming** for Tags to avoid confusion as your model grows.
- The **Tags panel** and **Outliner** are essential tools for navigating and managing complex models.
- **Scenes** save your camera position, visibility settings, and more—perfect for presentations and workflow efficiency.
- Updating a Scene overwrites the previous version; create new Scenes to preserve alternatives.
- Controlling visibility with Tags and Scenes improves **performance** and keeps your workflow **clean and professional**.
- Start tagging early and save Scenes often—it takes seconds and saves hours later.

modules.title: The 3D Warehouse and Extensions
modules.content:
## From Blank Screen to Building Blocks: Leveraging the 3D Warehouse

Imagine you’ve sketched a cozy living room in SketchUp—walls in place, windows drawn, even the couch outlined in 2D. Now you need a coffee table, a lamp, and a bookshelf. Drawing each from scratch could take hours. What if you could grab a ready-made coffee table, plop it in, and keep modeling instead of starting from zero? That’s exactly what the **3D Warehouse** offers: a vast online library of 3D models you can search, preview, and import directly into your SketchUp projects.

The 3D Warehouse isn’t just a convenience—it’s a game-changer for speed and creativity. Whether you're designing a home, a retail space, or a fantasy castle, you can fill your scene with realistic furniture, plants, vehicles, and architectural details without mastering every shape from scratch. Best of all, SketchUp and the 3D Warehouse are tightly integrated, making the process nearly seamless.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to tap into this resource, bring models into your project efficiently, and even tweak them to fit your design. You’ll also discover how to supercharge SketchUp with **extensions**—small plugins that add new features, automate tasks, or streamline workflows. By the end, you’ll move from building everything yourself to building smarter, faster, and with more confidence.

---

## Searching and Importing Models from the 3D Warehouse

### What is the 3D Warehouse?

The **3D Warehouse** is a free online repository hosted by Trimble (the company behind SketchUp) where users worldwide upload and share 3D models. It contains millions of models—from real-world furniture and appliances to stylized characters and fantasy objects. Most models are created by the SketchUp community and are available for non-commercial and commercial use under various licenses.

💡 **Pro Tip:** Always check the **license** of a model before using it. Some models are free for personal use only, while others can be used commercially. When in doubt, look for models labeled with a **Creative Commons license** or marked for commercial reuse.

### How to Access the 3D Warehouse

You can access the 3D Warehouse right from within SketchUp:

1. Open SketchUp.
2. Go to **File > 3D Warehouse > Get Models…** (on Windows) or **Window > 3D Warehouse > Get Models…** (on Mac).
3. A browser window will open to the [3D Warehouse website](https://3dwarehouse.sketchup.com), showing a search bar and featured models.

Alternatively, you can visit the 3D Warehouse directly in your web browser and download models to import later. This is useful if you want to browse on a tablet or review models before downloading.

### Searching for Models

Once in the 3D Warehouse:

- Type your search term in the top search bar—for example, “modern armchair” or “oak dining table.”
- Use filters to narrow results:
  - **Category:** furniture, architecture, vehicles, etc.
  - **Style:** modern, classic, cartoon, etc.
  - **Units:** meters or feet (match this to your SketchUp model’s units).
  - **License:** filter by usage rights.
- Click on a model thumbnail to view its details, including:
  - Preview images.
  - Model dimensions.
  - Number of faces (a rough indicator of complexity).
  - Author and license information.

📌 **Example:** Search for “Barcelona chair” and you’ll likely find several versions. Pick one with a CC license and clear dimensions.

### Downloading and Importing a Model

Once you’ve found a suitable model:

1. Click the **Download** button.
2. Choose whether to open the model directly in SketchUp or save it as a `.skp` file.
3. If you choose to open directly, SketchUp will launch (if not already open) and import the model into your current scene.
4. The model will appear in your scene, often centered on the origin.

💡 **Pro Tip:** If the model appears too large or too small, use the **Tape Measure tool** to check its scale. You can then use the **Scale tool** to resize it proportionally.

---

## Optimizing Imported Models to Improve Performance

Bringing in a detailed model—like a high-resolution sofa or a detailed car—can instantly add realism to your scene. But it can also slow down your SketchUp file, especially if you import multiple complex models. This slowdown happens because SketchUp has to process and render all those **faces** (the flat surfaces that make up the 3D shape).

### What Are Faces and Polygons?

A **face** in SketchUp is a flat surface bounded by edges. Every face is made of at least three edges, forming a triangle or polygon. The more faces a model has, the more detailed it looks—but the more power it takes to draw and edit it.

Models with **high polygon counts** (thousands or tens of thousands of faces) can make SketchUp laggy, especially on older or less powerful computers. They also increase file size, making it harder to share or export your project.

### How to Spot a High-Polygon Model

Look for these clues in the 3D Warehouse:

- **High number of faces** in the model details (e.g., 50,000+).
- **Curved surfaces** (like chairs with smooth cushions) often use many small faces to approximate the curve.
- **Detailed textures** (e.g., wood grain with fine details) also add hidden complexity.

📌 **Example:** A low-poly chair might have 100 faces. A high-poly version could have 10,000. The difference in realism is subtle in SketchUp’s default view, but the performance impact is huge.

### Ways to Optimize Imported Models

You don’t have to accept a model just as it is. Here are practical ways to simplify it:

#### 1. Simplify Geometry with the **Simplify Contours** Tool

SketchUp has a built-in tool to reduce unnecessary detail:

1. Select the imported model.
2. Go to **Window > Default Tray > Soften Edges**.
3. In the Soften Edges panel, check **Smooth normals**.
4. Adjust the **Angle** slider (try 30° to start).
   - This merges adjacent faces with similar normals, reducing the total face count.
5. Click **Soften Edges**.

This won’t remove all small details, but it can significantly reduce file size and improve performance.

#### 2. Use the **Sandwich Tool** (from Solid Tools)

If the model has unnecessary internal geometry (like a hollow chair with hidden back panels), you can use **Solid Tools** to clean it up:

1. Select the model.
2. Go to **Tools > Solid Tools > Sandwich**.
3. Use the **Push/Pull tool** to extrude a face inward, creating a solid.
4. Trim away unwanted parts.

This is more advanced but effective for reducing hidden geometry.

#### 3. **Explode and Rebuild** (Advanced)

For full control:

1. **Explode** the component (right-click > Explode).
   ⚠️ Warning: This breaks the model into individual edges and faces. Only do this if you’re comfortable rebuilding or simplifying.
2. Use the **Eraser tool** to remove unnecessary edges.
3. Rebuild key surfaces using the **Rectangle**, **Line**, and **Push/Pull** tools.
4. **Recreate as a Component** when done.
